titleText.es: Liarse con uno mismo: ¿ahora un tema oficial de xkcd? Inquietante.
titleText.en: Making out with yourself: now an official xkcd theme? Troubling.
titleText.noteEn: In Spain, liarse con alguien can colloquially mean to make out or hook up with that person.

regions.labelEs: NO DEBERÍA HACER ESTO, PERO TE HE TRAÍDO UN MOMENTO PARA DARTE UN CONSEJO.

applications.explanationEn: He is the present helper form for the speaker, and traído is traer’s completed-action form.
Para introduces the purpose, while dar remains in its unchanged dictionary form inside darte.
Te is attached to the end of the unchanged verb dar to identify the recipient.
Darte combines the action dar with the recipient te, and un consejo names one piece of advice.

regions.labelEs: ¿UN CONSEJO?
EQUIVÓCATE DE DIRECCIÓN, HABLA CON EXTRAÑOS, ABRE PUERTAS SIN LETRERO. Y SI VES A UN GRUPO DE GENTE EN UN CAMPO, VE A VER QUÉ ESTÁN HACIENDO. HAZ COSAS SIN SABER SIEMPRE CÓMO ACABARÁN.

applications.explanationEn: Equivócate is a positive command directed to one familiar listener.
The short marker te attaches to the positive command equivoca, and the written accent preserves the original stress.
Equivócate identifies the listener, de introduces the wrong choice, and dirección names that choice.
Habla is the positive command used with one familiar listener.
Abre is the positive command used with one familiar listener.
A appears before the group because the group consists of people receiving the action of ves.
Ve is the irregular positive command of ir for one familiar listener.
Qué introduces the unknown activity inside a larger statement, so it keeps its written accent without forming a separate direct question.
Están matches a plural group, and haciendo supplies the action in progress with its -iendo ending.
Haz is the irregular positive command of hacer for one familiar listener.
Sin introduces the absent action, and saber stays in its unchanged -er dictionary form.
Cómo introduces the unknown outcome inside a larger statement and therefore keeps its accent.
Acabarán keeps the full verb acabar and adds -án for what several things will do.

regions.labelEs: ¿POR QUÉ ME DICES ESTO?

applications.explanationEn: The two written words por qué ask for a reason, and qué carries an accent.

regions.labelEs: ERES CURIOSA Y LISTA Y ESTÁS ABURRIDA, TODO LO QUE VES ES UNA ELECCIÓN ENTRE TRABAJAR DURO Y GANDULEAR. HAY MUCHAS AVENTURAS QUE TE ESTÁS PERDIENDO PORQUE ESTÁS ESPERANDO A CONFECCIONAR UN PLAN. PARA ENCONTRARLAS, BUSCA PEQUEÑAS ELECCIONES INTERESANTES. Y RECUERDA QUE SIEMPRE ESTÁS CONSTRUYENDO EL FUTURO SOBRE LA MARCHA.

applications.explanationEn: Lo que refers to an unnamed set of things or experiences rather than a masculine noun.
Aventuras is what is missed, que points back to it, and te with perdiendo marks the listener as the person missing the experiences.
Estás matches the listener, and perdiendo supplies the ongoing action with its -iendo ending.
Porque is written as one unaccented word here because it introduces a reason.
Estás matches the listener, and esperando supplies the ongoing action with its -ando ending.
Esperando supplies the waiting action, a links it to the later action, and confeccionar stays in its dictionary form.
Para introduces the purpose, and encontrar remains in its unchanged form inside encontrarlas.
Las attaches to encontrar and identifies the feminine plural things to be found.
Busca is a positive command directed to one familiar listener.
Recuerda is a positive command directed to one familiar listener.
Estás matches the listener, and construyendo supplies the ongoing action with its -iendo ending.
The three words form the fixed expression for adapting or deciding while an activity is already underway.

regions.labelEs: PERO ESPERA, ¿QUÉ ES ESTE LUGAR? ¿VOY A DESPERTARME PENSANDO QUE ESTO ERA UN SUEÑO?

applications.explanationEn: Espera is a positive command directed to one familiar listener.
Voy matches the speaker, a links the two verbs, and despertar stays unchanged inside despertarme.
Me attaches to the end of despertar and identifies the speaker as the person who wakes up.
Era uses the imperfect because it presents the imagined dream as a background state rather than a bounded event.

regions.labelEs: ESTO ES... PIENSA EN ESTO COMO LO POSTERIOR AL JUEGO, EL EXTERIOR DEL TEATRO. PARA ENTRAR, TUVE QUE SUSPENDER LA INCREDULIDAD, OLVIDAR EL EXTERIOR.

applications.explanationEn: Piensa is a positive command directed to one familiar listener.
Lo turns posterior into a general aspect: the portion or state that comes afterward, without naming a masculine noun.
Para introduces the purpose, and entrar remains in its unchanged -ar dictionary form.
Tuve uses the preterite because it presents the obligation as a bounded event tied to entering.
Tuve changes for the speaker and past time, que links the obligation, and suspender stays unchanged.
The three words form the conventional expression for temporarily setting skepticism aside.

regions.labelEs: ENTONCES TÚ... EH. ¿POR QUÉ ME DAS CONSEJOS QUE VOY A OLVIDAR?

applications.explanationEn: The two written words por qué ask for a reason, and qué carries an accent.
Me identifies the recipient, das is the form of dar for the listener, and consejos names the advice.
Voy matches the speaker, a links the two verbs, and olvidar remains in its dictionary form.

regions.labelEs: OLVIDARÁS ESTE VIAJE, PERO CREO QUE LOS CONSEJOS SE QUEDARÁN CONTIGO.

applications.explanationEn: Olvidarás keeps the full verb olvidar and adds -ás for what one informal listener will do.
Quedarán keeps the full verb quedar and adds -án for what several things will do.

regions.labelEs: SI ESTO ES UN JUEGO, ¿ESTÁS--ESTAMOS--HACIENDO TRAMPA?

applications.explanationEn: The speaker switches from estás for “you are” to estamos for “we are”; both forms of estar lead to the same ongoing action haciendo.
Haciendo is the ongoing-action form of hacer, and trampa completes the fixed expression for cheating.

regions.labelEs: SÍ.
¿ESO ES UNA BUENA IDEA?
BUENO, ES UNA INTERESANTE. YA VEREMOS CÓMO VA.

applications.explanationEn: Una and interesante stay feminine because they point back to the previously mentioned feminine noun idea, which is not repeated.
Ya points toward a later resolution, and veremos supplies the future action of seeing how events develop.
Veremos keeps the full verb ver and adds -emos for what we will do.
Cómo introduces the unknown way the situation develops inside a larger statement, so it keeps its accent.

regions.labelEs: BUENO, SUPONGO QUE TE VERÉ POR AH...

applications.explanationEn: Veré keeps the full verb ver and adds -é for what the speaker will do.

regions.labelEs: ESPERA UN MOMENTO. ¿ME HAS TRAÍDO AQUÍ ANTES?

applications.explanationEn: Espera is a positive command directed to one familiar listener.
Un momento functions as an interruption when the speaker suddenly notices something.
Has is the present helper form for one familiar listener, and traído is traer’s completed-action form.

regions.labelEs: YO... QUIZÁS. UNA VEZ.
¿PARA OTRO CONSEJO?
EH...
EN REALIDAD, SOLO NOS LIAMOS.

applications.explanationEn: The fixed expression introduces a correction to the listener's assumption.
Nos marks a reciprocal action involving the pair, and liamos carries the informal Spanish-from-Spain romantic sense of liarse.

regions.labelEs: ¿NOS QU...
¡ADIÓS!

cards.noteEn: Esto is a neutral demonstrative for an unidentified thing, fact, or whole situation. It is not used directly before a noun.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.noteEn: Traído is the completed-action form, also called the past participle, of traer. It keeps the written accent on í.

cards.answerEn: Use para followed by the verb’s dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Use para + verb when the same person or thing performs both actions: in estudio para aprender, I both study and learn. When someone else performs the second action, Spanish needs the different pattern para que.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “in order to do something” in Spanish?

example.en: I study in order to learn.

cards.noteEn: Darte combines dar, the verb's unchanged dictionary form meaning “to give,” with te, meaning “to you.” The two parts are written as one word.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone gives another person advice?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of dar, identify the recipient with me, te, le, nos, or les, and add un consejo or consejos.
cards.noteEn: Dar changes for the person and time. The short recipient word normally comes before a changed verb, as in me dio, but it attaches to an unchanged dictionary form, as in darme. Spanish consejo is countable, while English advice usually is not.

example.es: Marta me dio un consejo útil.

cards.noteEn: Consejo is countable in Spanish: un consejo is one piece of advice and consejos is advice or several tips.

cards.answerEn: make a mistake; choose the wrong one (informal command)
cards.noteEn: Equivócate is a positive command to one familiar person. It combines equivoca with te and gains a written accent to preserve the spoken stress.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

cards.promptEs: imperativo afirmativo de tú + pronombre al final
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the command and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: A positive command tells someone to do something, rather than not to do it. With one informal listener, sienta + te becomes siéntate. A written accent may be added so the combined word keeps the original stress. In a negative command, the short word goes before the verb instead: no te sientes.
cards.questionEn: If a positive command includes a short word such as te (“yourself”) or lo (“it”), where does that word go?
How do you say that someone chooses the wrong door, road, number, or similar option?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of equivocarse, then de, then the option chosen incorrectly.
cards.noteEn: The short marker changes with the person: me equivoqué, te equivocaste, se equivocó. De introduces what was wrong. This pattern often sounds more natural than translating “wrong” with an adjective.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links equivocarse to the wrong choice
cards.noteEn: After equivocarse, de introduces what was chosen incorrectly: equivocarse de puerta means to choose the wrong door.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks a specific person as the object
cards.noteEn: Spanish generally places a before a specific person who receives a verb’s action. This “personal a” is not translated as a separate English word.

cards.promptEs: a + persona o expresión que se refiere a una persona
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes put a before the person affected by an action?
cards.answerEn: Put a before a person—or a word such as alguien or nadie—when that person directly receives the action.
cards.noteEn: This a is called the personal a. It is common before a named or specific person, but person-denoting words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) also take it. English usually has no separate word for it. Before the masculine article el, a + el contracts to al.
Ve is the irregular positive command of ir for one familiar person. It is different from ve meaning “he or she sees.”

cards.answerEn: to (linking a verb to the following infinitive)

cards.questionEn: When “what,” “how,” or “where” introduces unknown information inside a larger sentence, does Spanish keep the written accent?
cards.answerEn: Yes. Keep the accent in qué, cómo, dónde, cuándo, cuál, or quién even when the question is embedded inside a statement.
cards.noteEn: An embedded, or indirect, question reports what is unknown rather than asking it as a separate sentence. It may have no question marks, but the question word still carries its accent. Compare no sé dónde vive, “I don't know where she lives,” with the relative form donde in la casa donde vive, “the house where she lives.”

example.en: I don't know where she lives.

cards.answerEn: they are (helping to describe an action in progress)
cards.noteEn: Here están is the plural form of estar used before an action ending in -ando or -iendo.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by an action word ending in -ando or -iendo.
cards.noteEn: Estar changes to show who is doing the action: estoy, estás, está, and so on. For most verbs, replace -ar with -ando (hablar → hablando) and replace -er or -ir with -iendo (comer → comiendo, vivir → viviendo). This is similar to English “am/is/are doing.”
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is in the middle of doing something?

cards.noteEn: Haciendo is the -iendo form of hacer. Without a form of estar, it can describe how another action happens or what someone does at the same time.
Haz is the irregular positive command of hacer for one familiar person.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone does one thing without doing another?
cards.answerEn: Put sin before the second action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. When the same person performs both actions, Spanish uses sin directly before that form; it does not add a word equivalent to English “-ing.”

example.en: She left without closing the door.

cards.answerEn: they will end; they will turn out

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone will do in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Keep the action verb in its dictionary form and add a future ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The ending identifies the person: sentir plus -á gives sentirá, and ver plus -á gives verá. A few common verbs change their stem, but use the same endings.
Write the question form as two words, with an accent on qué. Write the usual answer word porque as one word without an accent.
cards.questionEn: How do you write “why” and “because” in Spanish?

example.es: ¿Por qué estudias español? Porque me gusta.
example.en: Why do you study Spanish? Because I like it.

cards.noteEn: Lista can mean “ready” in other contexts. When it describes a person as an ability, it means “smart” or “clever.”

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Lo combines with que to refer to an idea, action, or whole situation rather than a masculine noun. Together, lo que means “what” or “the thing that.”

cards.questionEn: How do you say “what” or “the thing that” without naming a specific object?
cards.answerEn: Use lo que to refer to an idea, action, situation, or unnamed thing.
cards.noteEn: Here lo is neutral: it does not stand for a masculine noun. Que introduces the information that identifies the idea or thing. Together they work as one unit.

example.en: I don't understand what you're saying.

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Here que completes lo que, a neutral expression meaning “what” or “the thing that.” It does not refer to a particular masculine or feminine noun.
In this comic, elección means a choice or decision rather than a political election.
After trabajar, duro describes the intensity of the work: trabajar duro means to work hard.
Gandulear is informal and describes spending time idly instead of working.

example.en: Today I want to laze around at home.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone misses an event, opportunity, or part of an experience?
cards.answerEn: Use perder with a matching me, te, se, nos, or os marker, followed by the thing missed.
cards.noteEn: The marker changes with the person: me pierdo, te pierdes, se pierde, nos perdemos. Here perderse does not mean becoming geographically lost; it means failing to experience something.

example.en: I don't want to miss the concert.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; marks a “you” verb used with te
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs use te when the person affected is the informal listener. The meaning belongs to the whole verb pattern, so English may not translate te separately.
With a matching me, te, se, or nos marker, perderse can mean to miss an event or opportunity, not only to become lost.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone waits before doing an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of esperar, then a, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir is called the infinitive. Esperar a hacer algo means to wait to do it. This differs from esperar hacer algo without a, which can mean to hope or expect to do it.

example.es: Esperó a terminar antes de responder.
example.en: She waited to finish before answering.

cards.answerEn: to put together; draw up; formulate
cards.noteEn: Confeccionar often means to make something by assembling its parts. With un plan, it means to draw up or formulate a plan.

example.en: The team drew up a list.

cards.noteEn: Encontrarlas combines encontrar, “to find,” with las, “them.” Las refers back to more than one feminine thing.

example.en: I hope to find them soon.

cards.noteEn: Here the plural elecciones means choices or decisions.

example.en: We make small choices every day.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of sobre la marcha (“as you go”)

cards.questionEn: What expression means doing or deciding something as you go, without planning every detail first?
cards.answerEn: Use sobre la marcha to mean “as you go” or “on the fly.”
cards.noteEn: The expression describes adapting, deciding, or learning during the activity itself rather than preparing everything in advance. Its meaning is broader than the literal meanings of sobre and marcha.

example.es: Decidiremos los detalles sobre la marcha.
example.en: We'll decide the details as we go.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of sobre la marcha (“as you go”)
progress; motion (in sobre la marcha, “as you go”)
Use a form of ir (“to go”), then a, then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Ir changes to match the person: voy a means “I am going to,” vas a means “you are going to,” and va a means “he/she is going to.” The final action stays in its unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form. This pattern expresses a plan, intention, or expected future event.
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is going to do something?

cards.answerEn: to (part of ir a + infinitive, going to do something)

cards.noteEn: Despertarme combines despertar with me. The me marks the speaker as the person who wakes up; English normally expresses the same idea with “wake up.”

example.en: I want to wake up early.

cards.noteEn: Era is a past form of ser used for a background state, description, or ongoing past situation. This form is called the imperfect.

cards.answerEn: Use the preterite for a completed event and the imperfect for background, an ongoing situation, or something that used to happen.
cards.noteEn: Think of a story: the preterite answers “What happened next?” The imperfect answers “What was happening?”, “What were things like?”, or “What used to happen?” These two names describe how the speaker presents an event, not simply how long it lasted.
cards.questionEn: Spanish has two common ways to talk about the past. When do you use each one?

example.en: While I was walking, it started to rain.

cards.answerEn: the (neutral article before an adjective, as in lo mejor)
cards.noteEn: Neutral lo turns an adjective into an abstract idea: lo importante means “the important thing,” not a masculine noun.

example.en: The important thing is to begin.

cards.questionEn: How do you refer to “what is important,” “the difficult part,” or another general quality without naming a noun?
cards.answerEn: Put the unchanged word lo before a masculine-singular adjective: lo importante, lo difícil, lo bueno.
cards.noteEn: Here lo does not stand for a masculine object. It turns the quality into a general idea or aspect, such as lo importante, “what is important.” The adjective stays in its masculine singular form because there is no named noun for it to match.
Al is the required contraction of a + el. Spanish writes them as one word whenever both occur together.
Del is the required contraction of de + el. It can mean “of the” or “from the,” depending on context.
Tuve is the completed-past form of tener for the speaker. This completed-event past is called the preterite.

cards.promptEs: tener que + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone has to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of tener, then que, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Only tener changes for the person and time: tengo que, tienes que, tiene que, and so on. The final action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes tener que, “to have to”

cards.questionEn: What expression means temporarily accepting an invented story instead of objecting that it is unrealistic?
cards.answerEn: Use suspender la incredulidad for “to suspend disbelief.”
cards.noteEn: The expression describes setting skepticism aside so that a play, film, game, or story can be enjoyed on its own terms. Suspender here means to pause or set aside, not to fail an exam.

example.es: La película invita a suspender la incredulidad.
example.en: The film invites you to suspend disbelief.

cards.noteEn: Consejos is grammatically plural in Spanish even when natural English simply uses the uncountable word “advice.”

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks quedarse, “to remain” or “stay”
cards.noteEn: Quedar and quedarse have several uses. With se here, the subject continues to be present rather than leaving.

cards.answerEn: they will remain; they will stay

cards.noteEn: Spanish combines con and ti into the special single word contigo.

example.en: I want to talk with you.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “to cheat” in a game, test, or competition?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of hacer followed by trampa.
cards.noteEn: Hacer changes for the person and time, while trampa normally stays singular in this expression. The phrase refers to breaking the rules for an unfair advantage.

example.es: Nadie hizo trampa en el examen.

cards.noteEn: With hacer, trampa means cheating or breaking the rules.
Buena has the feminine ending because it describes the feminine noun idea.
Idea ends in -a but is a feminine noun: una idea.

cards.promptEs: el/la/los/las o un/una + adjetivo sin repetir el sustantivo
cards.questionEn: How do you say “the interesting one” or “a small one” without repeating the noun?
cards.answerEn: Keep the article and adjective, omit the repeated noun, and make both agree with that understood noun.
cards.noteEn: The article is a word such as el, la, un, or una. The adjective still changes to match the omitted noun: una pequeña can mean “a small feminine one,” while uno pequeño can mean “a small masculine one.” Context supplies the missing noun.

example.es: Quiero una taza; dame la pequeña.
example.en: I want a cup; give me the small one.

cards.noteEn: An adjective can stand in for a noun that has just been mentioned. The surrounding article shows which omitted noun it describes.

example.es: Busco una película; quiero una interesante.
example.en: I am looking for a movie; I want an interesting one.

cards.answerEn: in due course; then (in ya veremos, “we'll see”)
cards.noteEn: Ya has several uses. In ya veremos, it suggests that time or events will reveal the answer later.

cards.questionEn: What can you say when the result is uncertain and time will show what happens?
cards.noteEn: The expression can be neutral, cautious, or noncommittal. Ya points toward a later resolution, and veremos is the future form meaning “we will see.”

example.en: Maybe it will work; we'll see.

cards.noteEn: Ir can describe how a situation develops. Cómo va can ask how something is going or how it turns out.

example.en: We'll see how the project goes.

cards.answerEn: around; over (in por aquí, “around here” or “this way”)
arou—; the interrupted beginning of ahí in por ahí (“around”)
cards.noteEn: The printed speech cuts ahí off after ah because the speaker interrupts themself. The complete expression te veré por ahí can mean “I'll see you around.”

cards.questionEn: What does ¡Un momento! mean when someone interrupts or suddenly realizes something?
cards.answerEn: It means “Wait a moment!” or “Hold on!”
cards.noteEn: This fixed conversational interruption can ask someone to pause, or it can announce that the speaker has just noticed something important. Its function is broader than literally measuring one moment.

example.es: ¡Un momento! Creo que tengo la llave.
example.en: Hold on! I think I have the key.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of en realidad (“actually”)

cards.noteEn: Use it to correct or qualify what someone may believe. It does not mean “currently”; Spanish normally uses actualmente for that meaning.
cards.questionEn: What expression means “actually” or “in fact” when correcting an impression?

example.es: Pensaba que era lunes, pero en realidad es martes.
example.en: I thought it was Monday, but it is actually Tuesday.

cards.answerEn: actually; in fact (as part of en realidad)
each other; marks a shared action involving “us”
cards.noteEn: With a plural verb, nos can show that the speakers do the action to or with each other. Context distinguishes this reciprocal use from nos meaning simply “us.”

cards.questionEn: In informal Spanish from Spain, how can you say that someone makes out or hooks up with another person?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of liarse, usually followed by con and the other person.
cards.noteEn: The short marker changes with the person: me lío, te lías, se lía, nos liamos. In this colloquial sense, the expression is about a romantic or sexual encounter. In other contexts, liarse can instead mean to get tangled, confused, or involved in a mess.

example.es: Se lió con alguien en la fiesta.
example.en: They hooked up with someone at the party.

cards.answerEn: we made out; we hooked up (informal, especially in Spain)
cards.noteEn: Liar normally means to tangle or make a mess. The pronominal expression liarse con alguien can colloquially mean to make out or hook up with someone.

example.es: Se lió con alguien de la fiesta.
example.en: They hooked up with someone from the party.

cards.answerEn: wh—; the interrupted beginning of qué (“what”)
cards.noteEn: The speaker is cut off before finishing qué. The fragment is not a separate Spanish vocabulary word.
